about: Overview

Motoring law covers the offences that can be committed by anyone who drives, rides or keeps a vehicle on a road or in a public place. Some are minor and are dealt with by a fixed penalty in the post. Others lead to a court hearing, penalty points, a driving ban and in the most serious cases a prison sentence. Almost all motoring cases in England and Wales start in the magistrates' court, and most finish there too.

For many people the real worry is not the fine. It is the licence. Losing the right to drive can affect a job, a business, caring for a relative or getting children to school. That is why people often look for a solicitor who deals with motoring cases every day, rather than a general high street firm or no help at all.

A specialist motoring solicitor will usually start by reading the paperwork, checking the dates and looking at the evidence the police or prosecutor relies on. They will then explain in plain terms what the likely outcomes are, whether there is anything to challenge, and what the court will be looking at. If you are pleading guilty, they can put forward mitigation, which is information about you and the offence that may help the court reach a fair sentence.

Motoring cases also move quickly and to fixed dates. A notice may give you a short time to reply, and a court date is rarely moved without a good reason. People who get in touch with a solicitor early tend to have more time to gather documents, find witnesses or arrange evidence about how a ban would affect them. Leaving it until the morning of the hearing narrows what anyone can do.

about: Leaflegal is not a law firm and does not give legal advice. We introduce you to one regulated firm that handles motoring cases. That firm looks at your own situation and tells you what your options are.
Points and bans

Most motoring offences are endorsable. That means a conviction is recorded on your driving record with an offence code and, for many offences, a number of penalty points. The number of points depends on the offence and sometimes on how serious the court thinks it was. Some offences have a fixed number of points and others have a range.

Points are counted under what is known as the totting up system. If you reach 12 or more points from offences committed within three years of each other, the court will usually disqualify you for at least six months. The minimum is longer if you have been banned before in the recent past. Points stay on your record for four years for most offences, and for eleven years for drink and drug driving related offences, even though only some of them count towards totting up.

Before passing sentence, the court will look at your driving record. Points that are still live for totting up purposes are taken into account, so an offence that would normally mean three points can have a much bigger effect if you already have nine. This is one reason people often check their record before deciding how to respond to a notice.

A ban can happen in more than one way. Some offences, such as drink driving, carry an obligatory ban, so the court must disqualify unless there are special reasons not to. For other offences the court has a discretion to ban instead of adding points, often where the offence was serious, such as a very high speed. And then there is the totting up ban, which comes from the build up of points over time rather than from one offence on its own.

Drivers in their first two years after passing their test have a lower limit. If they reach six points in that period, the DVLA will usually revoke their licence and they will need to apply for a provisional licence and pass the theory and practical tests again. This happens automatically and is separate from the court's own powers.

For some of the most serious offences, such as dangerous driving, the court must order an extended retest. The driver cannot simply get their licence back at the end of the ban. They need to pass a longer, harder test first.
The court process

Motoring cases follow the criminal court process in England and Wales. The details vary with the offence, but most cases go through the same broad stages. A solicitor will tell you where your own case is and what comes next.

For many offences caught on camera, the first thing you receive is a notice of intended prosecution and a request to name the driver. For offences where you were stopped, you may have been told at the roadside or charged at a police station. Cases then usually reach court by a postal requisition, a written charge with a Single Justice Procedure notice, or a charge sheet with a date to attend.

Many lower level motoring cases are dealt with by a single magistrate on the papers, without a hearing in open court. You are sent a notice and asked to respond within a set time, pleading guilty or not guilty and giving details of your finances. If you plead not guilty, or if a ban is being considered and you want to be heard, the case can be moved to a magistrates' court hearing.

At the first hearing in the magistrates' court you are asked to enter a plea. If you plead guilty, the court may sentence you there and then, or adjourn for reports or for a further hearing. If you plead not guilty, the court sets a trial date and gives directions about evidence.

Most hearings take place at the magistrates' court for the area where the offence happened, which may be some way from where you live. Hearings are usually listed for the morning or afternoon, and you may have to wait several hours to be called. Your solicitor can tell you what to expect on the day, where to go and what to bring.

At a trial, the prosecution has to prove the offence. Witnesses may give evidence and be cross examined. If you are found guilty, or have pleaded guilty, the court passes sentence using guidelines published by the Sentencing Council. A few serious offences, such as dangerous driving, can be sent to the Crown Court.
After a magistrates' court decision there is usually a right of appeal to the Crown Court, within a strict time limit. A solicitor can explain whether an appeal is possible and what it involves.
Choosing a firm

Motoring law is a specialist area. The rules on notices, time limits, evidence and sentencing are technical, and local courts each have their own way of doing things. Many people prefer a firm that handles motoring work as a main part of its practice.

list: How many motoring cases the firm deals with, and of what kind
Who will look after your case and who will attend court
Whether they will review the evidence before talking about plea
What the fee covers and what would cost extra
How they keep you updated before the hearing

about: It also helps to think about what you want from the firm. Some people want a quick review and a view on the likely outcome. Others want a solicitor to handle everything, from writing to the prosecutor to standing up in court. Being clear about this from the start makes it easier for the firm to give you an accurate fee.
Your solicitor may attend court themselves or instruct a barrister to represent you. Both are regulated. If a barrister is used, ask whether their fee is included in the price you have been given.

Every firm we introduce is regulated, usually by the Solicitors Regulation Authority. Regulated firms must be clear about costs, have a complaints procedure and hold insurance. You can check a firm on the regulator's online register.
Leaflegal introduces you to one firm, so you are not passed between lots of different companies. You are free to decide whether to instruct them.
Costs

Legal aid is rarely available for motoring cases, because it is usually only granted where there is a real risk of prison or other special factors. Most people pay privately for help with a motoring matter.

Many motoring firms charge fixed fees for each stage, such as an initial review, a guilty plea hearing, an exceptional hardship hearing or a trial. Others charge by the hour for complex cases. Trials cost more than guilty pleas because of the preparation and court time involved. Some cases also need expert evidence, such as a report on a speed device or a blood analysis, which is usually an extra cost.

If you are convicted, the court will usually order a fine, a victim surcharge and a contribution to the prosecution's costs. Fines for many offences are linked to your income. These amounts are set by the court and are separate from your solicitor's fees.

When you compare quotes, look at what is included rather than just the headline number. A low fee for a guilty plea may not include travel to a distant court, a barrister's fee or work on a separate exceptional hardship argument. A good firm will confirm the fee and what it covers in writing before any work starts.

If you are found not guilty, you may be able to recover some of your legal costs from public funds. The amount that can be recovered is usually limited and is often less than what you paid, so ask the firm how this works before you start.
Leaflegal is free to use. The firm pays us for the introduction, and that never changes what you pay them. The firm will explain its fees before you agree to anything.
What to prepare
Motoring cases move to fixed deadlines, so having the right information ready when the solicitor calls helps them give you a clear picture quickly.

list: Any notice, letter, charge sheet or court papers you have received, with every page
The date of the offence and the date of any court hearing
Your current points, which you can check on the GOV.UK driving licence service
Details of any previous bans
How you use your car, for work, family or health reasons
Any dashcam footage, photos or names of witnesses
Details of prescribed medicines, if relevant

about: If you have a response deadline on a notice, tell the firm straight away. Missing a deadline can create a separate offence or lead to a case being decided without you.
Try to be open with the solicitor about what happened, even the parts you are unsure of. What you tell them is confidential, and they can only help if they have the full picture.

If you think a ban would cause problems for other people, such as an employer, a relative you care for or your own staff, it can help to note down who they are and how they depend on your driving. Your solicitor can then explain whether that information is relevant and what kind of evidence the court usually expects to see.
faqs: General
What counts as a motoring offence?

A motoring offence is any criminal offence connected with driving, riding or keeping a vehicle. Common examples are speeding, drink and drug driving, using a mobile phone, careless driving, driving without insurance and failing to name the driver. Most are dealt with in the magistrates' court, and many lead to penalty points or a driving ban as well as a fine.
Do I need a solicitor for a motoring offence?

There is no rule that you must have one, and many people deal with a simple fixed penalty on their own. People often look for a solicitor when a ban is possible, when they think there is a problem with the evidence, or when their job depends on driving. A solicitor will look at your own situation and explain the options.
Does Leaflegal give legal advice?

No. Leaflegal is an introduction service, not a law firm, and does not give legal advice. We pass your enquiry to one regulated firm that handles motoring cases. Any advice you receive comes from that firm, and they will explain their fees before you decide whether to instruct them.
Which courts deal with motoring cases?

Almost all motoring cases in England and Wales begin in the magistrates' court. Many are decided by a single magistrate on the papers under the Single Justice Procedure. A small number of serious cases, such as dangerous driving or causing death by driving, can go to the Crown Court. Appeals from the magistrates' court usually go to the Crown Court.
Is a motoring conviction a criminal record?

Yes. A conviction for an endorsable motoring offence is a criminal conviction, although many people do not think of it that way. It will appear on your driving record and may need to be disclosed to insurers and some employers. How long it must be disclosed depends on the sentence and the rules on rehabilitation.
Will a conviction affect my insurance?

Usually yes. Insurers often ask about motoring convictions and points over the last few years, and premiums tend to rise after a conviction, especially for drink driving or a ban. Not telling an insurer when asked can cause problems if you later make a claim. Your insurer can tell you what they need to know.
Can a business be prosecuted for a motoring offence?

Yes, in some situations. A company that owns or keeps a vehicle must respond to a request to name the driver, and failing to do so is an offence. Businesses can also face prosecution over vehicle condition, loads or drivers' hours. Directors and fleet managers often ask a solicitor to review how their notices are handled.
Notices and court
What is a notice of intended prosecution?

It is a warning that you may be prosecuted for certain offences, such as speeding. For many offences it must be given at the time or sent to the registered keeper within a set number of days. It often comes with a request to name the driver. A solicitor can check whether the notice was served correctly.
What is a Single Justice Procedure notice?

It is a way of dealing with some lower level offences on paper. A single magistrate decides the case using the written evidence and your reply, without a hearing in open court. You are given a deadline to respond. If you plead not guilty or want to explain something in person, you can ask for a court hearing.
What happens if I ignore court papers?

Ignoring court papers rarely makes a case go away. The court may decide the case without you, which can mean a conviction, a fine, points or a ban that you only find out about later. In some cases a warrant can be issued. If you have missed a deadline, a solicitor can explain what options may still be open.
How long does a motoring case take?

It varies a lot. A guilty plea under the Single Justice Procedure can be finished within weeks of the reply. A case that goes to trial in the magistrates' court can take several months. Cases that need blood analysis or expert evidence often take longer. Your solicitor can give you a better idea once they see the papers.
Do I have to go to court?

It depends on the offence and how the case started. Some cases can be dealt with by post. Others require you to attend, especially where a ban is likely or where the court has said you must be there. Your solicitor can tell you whether you need to attend and can usually represent you when you do.
Can I appeal a magistrates' court decision?

There is usually a right of appeal to the Crown Court against conviction, sentence or both. The time limit is short, normally 21 days from the sentence. In some cases you can ask for a driving ban to be suspended until the appeal is heard. A solicitor can explain whether an appeal is realistic.
Can the police just send me a fixed penalty?

For many minor offences, yes. A fixed penalty lets you accept a set fine and, for endorsable offences, a set number of points without going to court. It is not always offered, for example where the offence is too serious or you would reach 12 points. You can usually choose to have the matter decided by a court instead.
What is a postal requisition?

A postal requisition is a formal document sent by post that tells you what you are charged with and when and where you must attend court. It is commonly used for drink and drug driving cases after the police have released you, and for other offences where a court hearing is needed. It usually comes with the prosecution's case summary.
Points and bans
How many points lead to a ban?

Under the totting up system, reaching 12 or more points from offences committed within three years of each other usually leads to a ban of at least six months. Drivers within two years of passing their test face a lower limit of six points, which normally means their licence is revoked by the DVLA rather than a court ban.
How long do points stay on my licence?

For most offences, points stay on your driving record for four years from the date of the offence or conviction, depending on the offence. Drink and drug driving related endorsements stay for eleven years. Only points from offences within three years of each other count towards a totting up ban, even if older ones still show on your record.
Can I keep driving until my court date?

In most cases, yes. A ban usually starts from the day the court imposes it, not from the date of the offence or the charge. There are some exceptions, such as where a court imposes an interim ban before sentence. Your solicitor can tell you whether anything affects your own case.
What is the difference between special reasons and exceptional hardship?

Special reasons are about the circumstances of the offence itself, such as a genuine emergency, and can allow a court not to add points or not to impose an obligatory ban. Exceptional hardship is about the effect a totting up ban would have on you and others. They are different arguments with different rules.
Will I need to retake my test?

Not after most bans. You usually get your licence back when the ban ends, although for some offences you need to apply to the DVLA. The court must order an extended retest for certain serious offences, such as dangerous driving, and can order a retest in other cases. New drivers who reach six points also need to pass again.
What is a drink drive rehabilitation course?

It is a course a court can offer when it bans someone for a drink driving related offence for 12 months or more. If the driver completes it within the time set by the court, their ban is reduced. The driver pays for the course. It is not usually available for drug driving, and the court decides whether to offer it.
How do I check how many points I have?

You can view your driving record online through the GOV.UK driving licence service, using your licence number and a few personal details. It shows current endorsements, offence dates and any bans. It is worth checking before you reply to a notice or speak to a solicitor, because people often misremember dates and the exact number of points they hold.
Costs and firms
How much does a motoring solicitor cost?

It depends on the offence, how complex it is and whether there is a trial. Many firms offer fixed fees for each stage, such as a guilty plea or an exceptional hardship hearing. Trials and cases needing expert evidence cost more. The firm will explain its fees and what they include before you agree to anything.
Is legal aid available for motoring offences?

Legal aid is rarely granted for motoring offences, because it usually depends on a real risk of prison or other special factors. Most people pay privately. If your case is serious enough that legal aid might be available, a solicitor can tell you and help you apply.
Can I get my costs back if I am found not guilty?

Sometimes. A court can order that some of your legal costs are paid from public funds if you are acquitted. The amount is usually limited to set rates and is often well below what you paid privately. Ask the firm to explain how this works before you decide how to proceed.
Does Leaflegal charge me anything?

No. Leaflegal is free to use. The firm we introduce you to pays us a fee for the introduction, and that fee never changes what you pay them. You only pay the firm if you decide to instruct them, and they will explain their fees first.
Can the firm help me prepare for a hearing even if I plead guilty?

Yes. Many people who plead guilty still use a solicitor to prepare and present mitigation, which is information about the offence and about you that the court can take into account when deciding the sentence. A solicitor can also explain what the court is likely to focus on and what documents may be useful to bring.
Using Leaflegal
How does the introduction work?

You fill in a short form about the offence, any dates you know and how many points you already have. We pass your enquiry to one regulated firm that handles motoring cases. They contact you to talk it through, explain your options in general terms and set out their fees. You then decide whether to go ahead.
How quickly will a firm contact me?

Firms aim to get in touch quickly, usually within one working day and often sooner, especially when there is a court date or a response deadline coming up. Please give a mobile number you can answer and mention any urgent dates in your enquiry so the firm can prioritise.
Do I have to instruct the firm?

No. There is no obligation. You can talk to the firm, hear what they say about your situation and their fees, and then decide. If you choose not to go ahead, you do not owe Leaflegal or the firm anything for the introduction.
Is what I tell you confidential?

We only share the details you give us with the firm we introduce you to, so that they can contact you about your enquiry. What you then tell the solicitor is protected by their duty of confidentiality. Our privacy policy explains how we handle your information.
What if my offence happened in Scotland?

Scotland has its own courts and procedures, which are different from those in England and Wales. The firms we introduce deal with cases in the courts of England and Wales. If your case is in Scotland or Northern Ireland, you would usually need a solicitor who practises there.
